content: Binocular vision refers to the ability to use both eyes together to perceive a single, cohesive image. The term binocular is derived from the Latin words bin (meaning two) and oculus (meaning eye). Having two eyes provides several distinct advantages over having just one. Firstly, it offers a backup eye in case one becomes damaged. Secondly, it expands the field of view; for instance, humans have a horizontal field of view of approximately 150 degrees with one eye, which increases to about 180 degrees when both eyes are used. Thirdly, binocular vision enhances the ability to detect faint objects through a phenomenon known as binocular summation. Lastly, it enables stereopsis, which is the precise depth perception achieved through the parallax created by the slightly different positions of the two eyes on the head. Binocular vision typically involves the fusion of the two images from each eye into a single image, a process known as binocular fusion. This prevents double vision and allows for a unified perception of the environment. Other phenomena associated with binocular vision include utricular discrimination (the ability to identify which eye received a monocular stimulus), eye dominance (where one eye's image takes precedence over the other), allelotropia (the averaging of visual directions from both eyes), and binocular rivalry (the alternation of perception when each eye is presented with significantly different images). In terms of field of view and eye movements, animals exhibit adaptations based on their ecological roles. Prey animals often have eyes positioned on opposite sides of their heads to maximize their field of view, sometimes achieving nearly 360-degree vision. Their eyes may move independently to further enhance this field. Predatory animals, on the other hand, have forward-facing eyes to prioritize stereopsis and depth perception, with their eyes typically moving together. Eye movements can be classified as versions (both eyes moving in the same direction) or vergences (eyes moving in opposite directions). Convergence occurs when the eyes move inward to focus on a closer object, while divergence happens when they move outward to focus on a more distant object. Binocular summation refers to the improved ability to detect stimuli when using both eyes compared to one. This occurs through two mechanisms: a statistical advantage of having two detectors and neural summation, where certain cells in the visual cortex receive input from both eyes simultaneously, resulting in greater activity than the sum of the individual inputs. Beyond summation, the two eyes can influence each other in several ways. For example, light entering one eye affects the pupil size of both eyes. Accommodation (the eye's focus) and vergence (eye alignment) are reflexively linked, so focusing on a near object with one eye causes the other eye to adjust similarly. Additionally, interocular transfer allows adaptation effects in one eye to influence the other. Utricular discrimination is the ability to determine which eye received a monocular stimulus when both eyes are open. Singleness of vision, achieved through binocular fusion, prevents confusion between the images from each eye. However, if fusion fails, double vision (diplopia) occurs. Fusion is distinct from stereopsis, as some binocular vision disorders, like strabismus, can preserve fusion while eliminating stereopsis. Fusion occurs within a limited area of visual space called Panum's fusional area, beyond which double vision arises. Eye dominance occurs when one eye's image takes precedence over the other's, particularly when aligning images outside Panum's fusional area. This is evident when pointing at a distant object; the dominant eye determines the perceived alignment. Stereopsis is the ability to perceive depth based on the parallax created by the two eyes' different positions. It can be quantitative, providing accurate depth perception for objects within Panum's fusional area, or qualitative, indicating relative depth for objects outside this area. At extreme distances, depth perception diminishes, and objects appear to lie on the fixation plane. Allelotropia describes the phenomenon where an object off the fixation plane has different visual directions in each eye, but when fused, it is perceived with a new visual direction, typically averaged between the two eyes. This perceived direction originates from a point called the cyclopean eye, which is usually closer to the dominant eye. Binocular rivalry occurs when the two eyes are presented with very different images. Perception alternates between the two images, with one dominating for a few moments before switching to the other. Disorders of binocular vision can arise when the eyes are not accurately aligned. The six extraocular muscles controlling each eye must work in harmony to maintain proper alignment. Minor imbalances in muscle strength or insertion can lead to a tendency for one eye to drift, especially when fatigued, a condition known as phoria. Phorias can be revealed using the cover-uncover test, where the movement of the uncovered eye indicates the type of phoria (e.g., exophoria, esophoria, hyperphoria, or hypophoria). Most people have mild phorias, which are normal. More severe misalignments, such as tropias (e.g., exotropia or esotropia), are forms of strabismus and can result in amblyopia (lazy eye). Vertical misalignments (hypertropia or hypotropia) and rotational misalignments (cyclotropias) are less common. In animals, the positioning of the eyes reflects their ecological needs. Predators, like cats, have forward-facing eyes with overlapping fields of vision to enhance depth perception. Herbivores, like horses, have laterally placed eyes with minimal overlap to maximize their field of view. These adaptations highlight the evolutionary significance of binocular vision in different species.
